comparisons.peer_topic: Resolution plan strategy and regulatory consequences
comparisons.peer_summary: Citi employs a single point of entry resolution strategy, subjecting parent equity and unsecured creditors to losses. Regulatory feedback has identified shortcomings in data integrity and derivatives unwind capabilities in its resolution plans. If regulators deem the plan not credible or if deficiencies are not remedied, Citi could face stricter capital, leverage, or liquidity requirements, restrictions on growth, or asset divestitures, negatively impacting its reputation and operations.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup and Bank of America both describe a single point of entry resolution strategy where the parent holding company enters resolution while subsidiaries remain operational, resulting in losses being borne by the parent's equity and unsecured creditors. BAC notes the FDIC could replace it with a bridge holding company where equity is held solely for creditors, leading to security holder losses (bac_2024_1A_P032_S002, bac_2024_1A_P033_S001). Citi explicitly states that under its single point of entry strategy, only Citigroup (parent) enters bankruptcy, and 'losses... would be imposed first on holders of Citigroup's equity securities and thereafter on its unsecured creditors' (c_2024_1A_P052_S001, c_2024_1A_P052_S002).

sentences.text: Also, the FDIC could replace Bank of America Corporation with a bridge holding company, which could continue operations and result in an orderly resolution of the underlying bank, but whose equity would be held solely for the benefit of our creditors.

If the Corporation is resolved under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code or the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority, third-party creditors of our subsidiaries may receive significant or full recoveries on their claims, while security holders of Bank of America Corporation could face significant or complete losses.

Under Citi's preferred "single point of entry" resolution plan strategy, only Citigroup, the parent holding company, would enter into bankruptcy, while Citigroup's material legal entities (as defined in the public section of its 2023 resolution plan, which can be found on the FRB's and FDIC's websites) would remain operational outside of any resolution or insolvency proceedings.

As a result, Citigroup's losses and any losses incurred by its material legal entity subsidiaries would be imposed first on holders of Citigroup's equity securities and thereafter on its unsecured creditors, including holders of eligible long-term debt and other debt securities.

comparisons.peer_topic: Resolution strategy impacts on security holders and capital support mechanisms
comparisons.peer_summary: Regulatory resolution strategies, including the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and the FDIC's single point of entry strategy under OLA, create greater risk of loss for Group Inc.'s security holders by transferring subsidiary losses to Group Inc. while providing full recoveries to third-party creditors of subsidiaries. To facilitate this strategy, the firm established Funding IHC and a Capital and Liquidity Support Agreement (CLSA) that provides liquidity but requires automatic forgiveness of funding notes and transfer of receivables upon severe liquidity deterioration, actions which materially and adversely affect Group Inc.'s liquidity and might trigger earlier bankruptcy proceedings. If the strategy succeeds, security holders could face significant or complete losses, whereas if it fails, Group Inc.'s financial condition would be adversely impacted.
comparisons.comparison: Both Bank of America and Goldman Sachs disclose that their preferred single point of entry resolution strategy, whether under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code or the FDIC's Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), results in significant or complete losses for parent company security holders while protecting third-party creditors of subsidiaries. BAC states that security holders could face 'significant or complete losses' while third-party creditors of subsidiaries receive recoveries (bac_2024_1A_P033_S001). Similarly, GS notes that losses at the subsidiary level would be transferred to Group Inc. and borne by security holders, resulting in 'significant and possibly complete losses' for Group Inc.'s security holders, while third-party creditors of subsidiaries receive full recoveries (gs_2024_1A_P147_S001, gs_2024_1A_P147_S002). GS further details that OLA allows the FDIC to disregard strict priority of creditor claims, a specific mechanism also implied in BAC's discussion of OLA outcomes.

sentences.text: If the Corporation is resolved under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code or the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority, third-party creditors of our subsidiaries may receive significant or full recoveries on their claims, while security holders of Bank of America Corporation could face significant or complete losses.
The FDIC's "single point of entry" strategy may result in our security holders suffering greater losses than would have been the case under a bankruptcy proceeding or a different resolution strategy.

Assuming Group Inc. entered resolution proceedings and support from Group Inc. or other resources available to its subsidiaries was sufficient to enable the subsidiaries to remain solvent, losses at the subsidiary level would be transferred to Group Inc. and ultimately borne by Group Inc.'s security holders, third-party creditors of Group Inc.'s subsidiaries would receive full recoveries on their claims, and Group Inc.'s security holders (including our shareholders, debtholders and other unsecured creditors) could face significant and possibly complete losses.

In that case, Group Inc.'s security holders would face losses while the third-party creditors of Group Inc.'s subsidiaries would incur no losses because the subsidiaries would continue to operate and would not enter resolution or bankruptcy proceedings.

As described in "Business - Regulation - Banking Supervision and Regulation - Insolvency of an IDI or a BHC," if the FDIC is appointed as receiver under OLA, the rights of Group Inc.'s creditors would be determined under OLA, and substantial differences exist in the rights of creditors between OLA and the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, including the right of the FDIC under OLA to disregard the strict priority of creditor claims in some circumstances, which could have a material adverse effect on our debtholders.

comparisons.peer_topic: Resolution plan requirements, loss absorption strategy, and associated risks
comparisons.peer_summary: JPMorganChase must submit periodic resolution plans for orderly bankruptcy without government support, with failures potentially leading to stricter capital requirements, operational restrictions, or forced divestitures. The company's preferred single-point-of-entry strategy requires maintaining minimum eligible long-term debt to absorb losses first in equity and unsecured creditors, though the FDIC has not formally committed to this strategy, creating uncertainty that alternative approaches could result in greater losses for these holders.
comparisons.comparison: Both BAC and JPMorgan Chase explain that their single-point-of-entry resolution strategies subject parent equity holders and unsecured creditors to losses first. BAC discloses that its 'single point of entry' strategy may result in security holders suffering greater losses than under bankruptcy, with parent equity held solely for creditors (bac_2024_1A_P032_S002, bac_2024_1A_P032_S003). JPMorgan confirms that under its resolution strategy, losses are imposed first on holders of the Parent Company's equity securities and thereafter on unsecured creditors, including eligible long-term debt (jpm_2024_1A_P038_S001, jpm_2024_1A_P039_S002). Both firms highlight that this structure prioritizes the continuity of operating subsidiaries at the expense of the parent's investors.

sentences.text: The FDIC's "single point of entry" strategy may result in our security holders suffering greater losses than would have been the case under a bankruptcy proceeding or a different resolution strategy.

If the Corporation is resolved under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code or the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority, third-party creditors of our subsidiaries may receive significant or full recoveries on their claims, while security holders of Bank of America Corporation could face significant or complete losses.

As a result, the Parent Company's losses and any losses incurred by its subsidiaries would be imposed first on holders of the Parent Company's equity securities and thereafter on its unsecured creditors, including holders of eligible LTD.

If the Parent Company were to enter into a resolution, holders of eligible LTD, other unsecured creditors and holders of equity securities of the Parent Company will absorb the losses of the Parent Company and its subsidiaries.

comparisons.peer_topic: Resolution Planning, TLAC, and Regulatory Constraints on Capital Actions
comparisons.peer_summary: The firm must submit biennial resolution plans and is subject to potential stringent capital requirements or divestiture if plans are deemed non-credible; the likely resolution strategy is Single Point of Entry (SPOE), where the Parent Company provides capital to subsidiaries via a secured support agreement, potentially seniorizing subsidiary claims over unsecured parent debt. Regulators require the firm to maintain adequate Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) to absorb losses upon failure without government support; foreign 'bail-in' powers and potential subsidiary TLAC requirements may increase consolidated capital needs and restrict efficient capital distribution among affiliates. Consequently, the firm's ability to pay dividends or repurchase stock is subject to regulatory constraints, capital planning submissions to the Federal Reserve, stress test results, and potential changes in capital requirements that may restrict capital actions.
comparisons.comparison: Morgan Stanley aligns with Bank of America on the risks of the FDIC's Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) and Single Point of Entry (SPOE) strategy. BAC warns that OLA and SPOE may result in security holder losses (bac_2024_1A_P032_S003, bac_2024_1A_P033_S001). MS similarly states that the FDIC may apply OLA powers, which include the power to 'disregard the priority of creditor claims,' adversely impacting unsecured debt holders, and identifies the SPOE strategy as the 'reasonably likely outcome' if OLA is applied to a G-SIB (ms_2024_1A_P062_S002, ms_2024_1A_P063_S001). Both highlight the specific risk that OLA powers differ from standard bankruptcy priority protections.

sentences.text: The FDIC's "single point of entry" strategy may result in our security holders suffering greater losses than would have been the case under a bankruptcy proceeding or a different resolution strategy.

When a G-SIB such as Bank of America Corporation is in default or danger of default, the FDIC may be appointed receiver to conduct an orderly liquidation, and could, among other things, invoke the orderly liquidation authority, instead of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, if the Secretary of the Treasury makes certain financial distress and systemic risk determinations.

The FDIC's power under the orderly liquidation authority to disregard the priority of creditor claims and treat similarly situated creditors differently in certain circumstances, subject to certain limitations, could adversely impact holders of our unsecured debt.

Further, because both our resolution plan contemplates an SPOE strategy under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and the FDIC has indicated that it expects to use an SPOE strategy through which it may apply its orderly liquidation authority powers for a U.S. G-SIB, we believe that the application of an SPOE strategy is the reasonably likely outcome if either our resolution plan were implemented or a resolution proceeding were commenced under the orderly liquidation authority.
